title: lower() and casefold() disagree on the same Greek word
assumption: casefold() is just a more aggressive lower(), so it can only make more strings equal, never fewer, and never disagree with lower() about how to spell an individual word.

input.description: Comparing a Greek name typed in all caps against its lowercase spelling, or canonicalizing Greek text for a search index.

what_goes_wrong: word.lower() produces "\u03bf\u03b4\u03c5\u03c3\u03c3\u03b5\u03c5\u03c2" (ending in final sigma \u03c2, the form Greek orthography requires at the end of a word), but word.casefold() produces "\u03bf\u03b4\u03c5\u03c3\u03c3\u03b5\u03c5\u03c3" (ending in plain sigma \u03c3) — two different strings from the exact same input, so lower() == casefold() is False for this word.
why: Greek has two lowercase forms of sigma: \u03c3 inside a word and \u03c2 at the end of a word. Python's str.lower() applies the Final_Sigma rule from SpecialCasing.txt, a context condition (the sigma follows a cased letter and is not followed by one) that picks \u03c2 for the last letter here. str.casefold() exists for caseless MATCHING and uses CaseFolding.txt, which maps \u03a3, \u03c3 and \u03c2 all to \u03c3 with no context, so that words differing only in sigma form compare equal. JavaScript has no casefold(), so it has no built-in way to show this disagreement; its toLowerCase() applies the same Final_Sigma rule and matches Python's lower().
fix: Do not assume casefold() is a strict superset of lower()'s equalities, or that it preserves orthographic rules — it is only guaranteed to make caseless comparison consistent, not to produce "correctly spelled" lowercase text. For display, use lower(); for comparison, use casefold(); never mix the two results together or assert they're interchangeable.

sources.title: Unicode Standard: SpecialCasing.txt (Greek final sigma rule)
